presentingComplaint: Sudden-onset severe sore throat with fever for 2 days, initially thought to be glandular fever
history: A 19-year-old female college student presents with an abrupt onset of severe sore throat, odynophagia, high-grade fever and headache over 2 days. She has associated nausea with one episode of vomiting. There is NO cough, no rhinorrhoea/coryza, no hoarseness and no conjunctivitis. A roommate was recently treated for 'strep throat'. She initially attended a walk-in clinic where infectious mononucleosis was suspected (a friend had recently had glandular fever with prolonged fatigue), and a heterophile antibody (monospot) test was requested. However, she reports no significant fatigue preceding the illness, no left upper-quadrant discomfort. No prior tonsillectomy. No drug allergies. Not sexually active recently; no risk factors for gonococcal pharyngitis. This overlapping picture (exudative tonsillitis with tender nodes) raised infectious mononucleosis as the leading alternative, but the acute febrile onset, absence of cough/coryza, anterior (not posterior) cervical nodes and absence of splenomegaly point to Group A streptococcal pharyngitis, later confirmed.
examination: Alert, mildly flushed, not toxic. Oropharynx: markedly erythematous tonsils with bilateral creamy-white tonsillar exudate; a few palatal petechiae; no unilateral tonsillar bulge, no uvular deviation and no trismus (excludes peritonsillar abscess). Tender, enlarged ANTERIOR cervical lymph nodes bilaterally; no posterior cervical or generalised lymphadenopathy. No hepatosplenomegaly on abdominal exam. No rash/scarlatiniform eruption at presentation. Chest clear.
imaging: Not indicated; no imaging performed (no features of deep neck space infection).
microbiology: Rapid antigen detection test (RADT) for Group A Streptococcus: POSITIVE. Throat swab culture: Streptococcus pyogenes (group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus). Monospot negative and no atypical lymphocytosis, arguing against EBV infectious mononucleosis.
differentialDiagnoses: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV) — the principal mimic given exudative tonsillitis and cervical adenopathy
Peritonsillar abscess (excluded: no trismus, uvular deviation or unilateral swelling)
finalDiagnosis: Group A streptococcal (bacterial) acute pharyngitis — McIsaac/Centor score 4 (fever >38C, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, absence of cough), RADT and culture confirmed; infectious mononucleosis excluded by negative monospot and absence of posterior adenopathy/splenomegaly/atypical lymphocytosis.
citations: IDSA — Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis — 2012
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition — Pharyngitis and Streptococcus pyogenes infections
stewardship: Confirmed GAS pharyngitis warrants narrow-spectrum therapy to prevent acute rheumatic fever and suppurative complications. First-line: oral penicillin V 500 mg BD (or amoxicillin 500 mg BD) for 10 days. Amoxicillin is deliberately AVOIDED empirically if mononucleosis is not yet excluded because it can precipitate a florid maculopapular rash in EBV infection — here EBV is excluded, so a beta-lactam is appropriate. Macrolide (azithromycin) reserved for penicillin allergy. Antibiotics are NOT indicated for viral pharyngitis; confirmatory testing before treating avoids unnecessary prescribing.
contraindications: Avoid empirical aminopenicillins (amoxicillin/ampicillin) if infectious mononucleosis is not excluded — high risk of drug rash
Penicillin allergy: use a macrolide (azithromycin) or first-generation cephalosporin if non-anaphylactic
edgeCases: Overlap with infectious mononucleosis: exudative tonsillitis plus adenopathy can be either; posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly, marked fatigue and atypical lymphocytosis favour EBV
Co-infection: a positive RADT does not exclude concurrent EBV; both can coexist
Beware unilateral swelling, trismus or 'hot potato' voice signalling peritonsillar abscess requiring drainage
expectedMaiK: Acute sore throat with fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes and absence of cough (McIsaac 4) plus positive RADT/culture indicates Group A streptococcal pharyngitis; treat with a 10-day narrow-spectrum penicillin.
expectedNextQuestions: Is there cough, coryza or conjunctivitis (would favour a viral cause)?
Are the enlarged nodes anterior or posterior, and is there splenomegaly or profound fatigue (would favour EBV)?
Any prior rheumatic fever, penicillin allergy, or recent sick contacts with strep throat?
Any trismus, drooling or unilateral throat swelling suggesting peritonsillar abscess?
expectedInvestigations: Rapid antigen detection test (RADT) for Group A Streptococcus
Throat swab culture (confirm/backup where RADT negative in high-risk)
Heterophile antibody (monospot) / EBV serology to exclude infectious mononucleosis
Full blood count with film (atypical lymphocytes suggest EBV)

investigations: Rapid antigen detection test (RADT) for Group A Streptococcus

antibiotics: Penicillin V 500 mg PO BD for 10 days (or Amoxicillin 500 mg PO BD)

regressionAssertions: Engine must return PHARYNGITIS as the top diagnosis
Positive RADT/culture with McIsaac 4 must trigger antibiotic recommendation (narrow-spectrum penicillin)
Must not recommend broad-spectrum agents for uncomplicated GAS pharyngitis
